body.objective: Students will be able to interview a client and set requirements.
body.iCan: I can interview a client and set requirements.
successCriteria: I can interview a client to find their needs
I can write clear, measurable requirements and a proposal
I can plan deliverables and deadlines
body.hook: In the workplace, you don't build what you want; you build what the client needs, on their timeline and budget. The most important design skill at the advanced level isn't technical. It's listening.

study.title: Working for a Client
study.question: How do professionals turn a client's needs into a project plan?
study.passage:
Client options: a teacher or school department (posters for an event, a catered lunch, shelving for a classroom, a website for a club), a local business or community group, or a simulated client card from the teacher.
Part 1, Prepare (10 minutes): Write eight open questions. Examples: What problem are you trying to solve? Who will use it? What does success look like? What's your budget? When do you need it? What must it not be? Can you show examples you like?
Part 2, Interview (15 minutes): Listen more than you talk. Take notes. Repeat back key points to confirm ("So you need 40 lunches, nut-free, by noon Friday?").
Part 3, Requirements (10 minutes): Turn notes into 5 to 8 measurable requirements and note what is out of scope.
Part 4, Proposal (20 minutes): Write a one-page proposal: project summary, requirements, deliverables with deadlines, cost estimate, two design options with sketches, and a sign-off line.
Scope creep: when clients add requests after agreement, record the change and its effect on cost and time before agreeing.
study.source: Original client project task written for this lesson.
discussion: What did you learn from the interview that you wouldn't have guessed?
How do you handle a client who wants more than the budget allows?
What is scope creep and why is it risky?
study.product: Conduct a client interview and submit interview notes, a requirements list with scope, and a signed (or teacher-approved) one-page proposal.

examples.title: Open question
examples.problem: Rewrite "Do you want it blue?" as an open question.
examples.answer: "What colours or feelings should the design have?"

examples.title: Requirement
examples.problem: Client: "Lunch for the staff meeting." Make it measurable.
examples.answer: 40 nut-free lunches delivered by 11:45 a.m. Friday, under $8 each

examples.title: Scope creep
examples.problem: The client now wants dessert too. What do you do?
examples.answer: Note the added cost and time, get approval before agreeing

examples.title: Deliverables
examples.problem: List deliverables for a club website.
examples.answer: Home page, events page, contact form, admin guide

practice.q: How should you handle scope creep?
practice.a: Record the change, its cost and time, and get approval.
So both sides can agree when the project is complete.

practice.q: What if a client's budget can't meet their wishes?
practice.a: Explain trade-offs and offer options within budget.

practice.q: How does client work differ from personal projects?
practice.a: Decisions serve the client's needs, not your preferences.

misconceptions: Assuming you know what the client wants without asking
Agreeing to every new request without discussing cost and time
Thinking the proposal is just paperwork
